> I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes.

comments.text:
I'm curious, for someone more familiar with Goose: how do you represent an arbitrary number of dynamically sized values? If you have a fixed number of stacks, it seems like only a fixed number of values can change size at any given time.
For instance, how would you represent a hash table where the values are strings and at random, the program inserts or deletes a random string?
This doesn't seem like something you could easily represent. The only way I can think of is to keep a stack that holds all of your strings, and you periodically compact it.
Edit: Maybe you could also have a separate stack for strings of various sizes. One each for strings less than 8, 16, ... bytes. But at that point you're basically implementing your own malloc by hand.
Edit: Fwiw I do think Goose is very cool! I've had to hand-roll a lot of similar stuff in Rust before to speed up memory management

comments.author: pradn
comments.text:
Goose is pretty cool. The idea is that you don’t need to make representable all programs: a language for a restricted purpose is ok. As long as you can statically specify the number of growable memory regions, you can use Goose. However, since there’s no garbage collection, you’ll probably need to be careful about memory use while a program is running. Ie: the stacks can get too big if you keep growing them, even as old data is not used any more.
Still, for a large number of programs - like data-oriented applications - it’s probably a good fit. It might work ok with entity-component game systems as long as you reuse old memory…

comments.author: fasterik
comments.text:
So many entry-level explanations of quantum mechanics start with classical physics, waves, particles, the double-slit experiment, etc. and then jump straight to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. In my opinion, there's way too much conceptual baggage that comes with these concepts [0].
As a non-physicist, QM only clicked for me when I learned the linear algebra of one- and two-qubit systems and observables on those systems [1]. The math is accessible at a pre-calculus level, and the most "counter-intuitive" aspects of QM (interference, the uncertainty principle, entanglement) make perfect sense in this framework. I think it's the best starting point for understanding what QM really says.
[0] That's not to say they aren't important historically or for a complete understanding of QM. I'm talking about conceptual understanding for someone, especially a non-physicist, encountering QM for the first time.
[1] Chapter 2 of Nielsen and Chuang is what did it for me. It's heavygoing if you've never seen linear algebra before, but I don't know of a clearer explanation of the postulates of quantum mechanics.

comments.author: piterrro
comments.text:
Having used D1 in production - it's not very reliable. There was a comment on HN from one of D1 devs [1] saying that D1 is a sql wrapper on top of durable objects that mimicks sqlite distributed like nature.
> I'll let you in on a sort of dirty secret:
It's almost always better to use Durable Objects storage, rather than D1. Even if you only want a single global database, it's better to implement that as a singleton Durable Object, than by using D1. Because that's all D1 itself actually is: a singleton Durable Object that exposes an API to its SQLite database. It's just a wrapper.
[1]
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48611834

comments.author: gregsadetsky
comments.text:
I feel like there should be a comparison table listing all of these engines and how they compare on their external dependencies, whether a single leader/any node can write, their shape (embeddable library vs server), etc.
IMHO support for transactions is a pretty important dividing line. Some engines support full SQLite transactions while others - like rqlite - don't officially support BEGIN/COMMIT [0], which matters if you rely on multi-statement transactions.
A friend/colleague has been building a pure-Python client for dqlite [1] (DB-API and SQLAlchemy), which may interest folks here. dqlite has full support for transactions, and like rqlite doesn't have external dependencies (ie no S3/Consul).
No knock on rqlite or any other engine - dqlite has warts too [2].

comments.author: miki123211
comments.text:
I am a Python programmer. I love Astral; I think Ruff is great and uv is life-changing, but I don't actually like ty that much.
I want my type checker to check types and to scream at me when it can't. I don't want it to do "gradual typing", if it is unsure about what type something is, I want that to be a failure instead of it modeling the unsureness and not showing potential errors. We live in the age of agents, having to add an extra annotation here and there is not so much of a problem any more.
Meta's Pyrefly largely does what I want. I don't quite love Pyrefly either; I don't like the fact that it edge-cases and gives monopoly status to some popular packages (Pydantic, Django, attrs) instead of offering generalized mechanisms that less popular packages could also utilize, but purely on a type checking front, it's excellent.

comments.text:
Ah, this is great! It's a step towards solving my biggest complaint with PEP 723 scripts: bad editor support.
I loved the idea on paper, but without manually creating a matching venv & installing my deps, I wouldn't get in-editor completions during development. That was fine for small things, but intolerable as the script grew. So it's still not a feature I've used much, since it made more sense to just make a real dev environment.
I'm glad to see there'll be improvements here!
